extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, students of fiction, and literary practitioners studying narrative method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and handling narrative presentation in a novel — deciding between pictorial/panoramic and scenic/dramatic methods, managing point of view (subjective vs. authorial), and structuring episodes and perspectives so the story yields the intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject as interaction of character and environment
rubrics_metrics.description: What he proposes to exhibit is the history of a woman like her in just such a world as hers, a foolish woman in narrow circumstances; so that the provincial scene, acting upon her, making her what she becomes, is as essential as she is herself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat character and setting as mutually constitutive: the environment must be integral to the subject; the protagonist is not the sole focus but one pole of a relationship with her world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish portrait (study of character) from drama (conflict of wills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not a portrait, therefore, not a study of character for its own sake, but something in the nature of a drama, where the two chief players are a woman on one side and her whole environment on the other — that is Madame Bovary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the work is primarily pictorial (an impression/portrait) or dramatic (a conflict with a decisive issue). The choice determines emphasis: action/plot versus depiction/texture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Events may be illustrative rather than essential
rubrics_metrics.description: None of the events really matter for their own sake; they might have happened differently, not one of them is indispensable as it is. The events ... are only Flaubert’s way of telling his subject, of making it count to the eye. They are not in themselves what he has to say, they simply illustrate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the aim is pictorial, episodes can be chosen for their illustrative value rather than causal necessity; don't force every incident to carry plot indispensability if the goal is impression and character-picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial aim: render character and setting vividly and integrally
rubrics_metrics.description: It is pictorial, and its object is to make Emma’s existence as intelligible and visible as may be. She herself must be known thoroughly — the movement of her mind is to be watched at work... and the dull and limited world in which her appetite is somehow to be satisfied ... is to be rendered, and in order to make it clearly tell beside the figure of Emma it must be as distinct and individual, as thoroughly characterized as she is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the novel's purpose is to create a picture, devote equal detailing to setting and supporting figures; render the protagonist's inner life and the world with similar thoroughness so the impression is complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of point of view; avoid arbitrary shifting
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is to have that unity which it needs to produce its right effect there can be no uncertainty here, no arbitrary shifting of the place from which an onlooker faces it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and maintain a coherent center of vision. Random or blunt shifts of narrative stance undermine unity and reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enter consciousness when showing subjective experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of his subject is Emma’s sense of her world; we must see how it impresses her and what she makes of it ... For this reason it is essential to pass into her consciousness, to make her subjective; and Flaubert takes care to do so as soon as she enters the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To convey a character's inner life authentically, inhabit their consciousness in the narration; show how the world appears and affects them from within.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author must supply external view when protagonist's perception is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Her intelligence is much too feeble and fitful to give a sufficient account of her world... The author’s wit, therefore, and none other, must supply what is wanting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a protagonist lacks the perception to reveal necessary aspects of the world, the narrator should provide complementary, external rendering — but do so carefully to avoid jarring transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguise transitions between subjective and authorial perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: The transition must be made without awkwardness, without calling attention to it... There is nothing more disconcerting in a novel than to see the writer changing his part in this way — throwing off the character into which he has been projecting himself and taking a new stand outside and away from the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smoothly modulate shifts from character-focused subjectivity to authorial overview; avoid abrupt, self-conscious changes of voice that break the reader's immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep character at a certain distance to prevent complete identification
rubrics_metrics.description: He deals with the difficulty... by keeping Emma always at a certain distance, even when he appears to be entering her mind most freely. He makes her subjective... but he does so with an air of aloofness that forbids us ever to become entirely identified with her.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a controlled emotional distance when necessary so readers can observe and judge the character; this is particularly useful for characters whose inner life is limited or whose folly the author wants to ironize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use irony to modulate valuation without overt authorial assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: His irony, none the less, is close at hand and indispensable... His valuation of her is only implied; it is in his tone — never in his words, which invariably respect her own estimate of herself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imply authorial judgment through tone and ironic distance rather than explicit denunciation; let characters' own words stand while the narrator's tone frames their significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show protagonist from others' viewpoints to situate them in the world
rubrics_metrics.description: Some glimpse of her appearance in the sight of those about her — this, too, we look for... What did he really think of her, how did she appear to him? Light on this question not only makes a more solid figure of her for the reader, but it also brings her once for all into the company of the people round her.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include other characters’ perspectives to round out a protagonist's portrait and to prepare later narrative developments (e.g., a husband's discovery at the end).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame the main subject using parallel or surrounding narrative material
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole book, mainly the affair of Emma herself, is effectively framed in this other affair, that of Charles, in which it opens and closes. Madame Bovary is a well-made book... pulling it to pieces and putting it together again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use framing subplots, backstory, or parallel narratives to open and close the main subject, thereby strengthening structural unity and thematic resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish panoramic (survey) from scenic (dramatic) presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between the 'panoramic' and the 'scenic' presentation of a story... Thackeray saw them as broad expanses, stretches of territory, to be surveyed from edge to edge with a sweeping glance; he saw them as great general, typical impressions of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize whether the story needs panoramic survey (broad social/manners portrait) or scenic immediacy (dramatic enactment), and select the presentation mode accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use panoramic method to convey society, manners and a wide impression
rubrics_metrics.description: The book is not the story of any of them, it is the story which they unite to tell, a chapter in the notorious career of well-to-do London... Thackeray preferred the manner of musing expatiation, where scene melts into scene, impressions are foreshortened by distance...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ panoramic narrative, retrospective recollection, and broad generalizing when the aim is to capture a collective or social picture rather than a single tight plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panoramic technique: memory-based, fusion of detail, foreshortening
rubrics_metrics.description: He wrote his novel with a mind full of a surge and wash of memories... Briefly, to all appearance quite casually, the little incident shows itself and vanishes; the stream sets forward again, by so much enriched and reinforced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panoramic narration often works through associative memory, quick illustrative flashes, and selective foreshortening of scenes rather than continuous dramatization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Switch to scenic method for climactic, decisive moments
rubrics_metrics.description: The final scene cannot be recalled and summarized in his indirect, reminiscential manner. It must be placed immediately before us... The method that was not demanded by the preceding phases of the tale is here absolutely prescribed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve immediate, enacted scenes for moments that require close dramatic force or decisive answers; panoramas and summaries will blunt climaxes that need direct presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use immediate scenes for the answer or decisive action
rubrics_metrics.description: Becky, Rawdon, Steyne, must now take the matter into their own hands and show themselves without any other intervention... they must come forward, declare themselves, and be seen for what they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the narrative question demands a verdict or a concrete outcome, dramatize it through direct scene-playing by the characters themselves rather than authorial summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make episodes functional — they must serve the book's larger purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The chapters representing Becky’s manner of life in Curzon Street make the hinge of her career... Functional, therefore, they are to the last degree; but up to the very climax there is no need for a set scene of dramatic particularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design episodes so they contribute to structural pivots or thematic development; even descriptive or panoramic passages should be judged by their function in the larger design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict variety of method to the bare needs of the book; practice economy
rubrics_metrics.description: A book that with its variety of method, and with its careful restriction of that variety to its bare needs, and with its scrupulous use of its resources — it is a book, altogether, that gives a good point of departure for an examination of the methods of fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diverse narrative techniques sparingly and only when they serve the essential requirements of the subject; excessive variation weakens unity and effect.
